header: Chiral Boron Chemistry. Organoboron compounds occupy an important niche in asymmetric synthesis and have become versatile stereospecific building blocks. In general, the boron atom is an electron-deficient center; therefore, the most important intermediates in these reactions are boronate anions (ate complexes).

10.1.1 An ate-complex intermediate is formed in the reaction. Write the SMILES representations of the 2 key boron-containing intermediates in the transformation, including stereochemistry.

text_images.description: The image shows a one-step Matteson homologation. The reactant is 'C[C@H]1[C@H](C)OB(C)O1', and the conditions are 1) CH_2Cl_2, LDA; 2) ZnCl_2; 3) RMgBr. The product is 'C[C@H]1[C@H](C)OB([C@@H](C)[R])O1'.

subquestions.text_open: 10.1.2 Studies show that the addition of ZnCl_2 is the key step controlling the stereospecificity of the product. ZnCl_2 acts as a chelating agent and forms a 5-membered chelate ring, and the principal factor affecting the stability of the migration transition state is 1,3-strain between bulky groups. On this basis, write the SMILES representation of the key intermediate leading to the major product, including stereochemistry.

10.1.3 If CH_2Cl_2 in the first step is replaced with CH_3CHCl_2, the stereoselectivity of the product will: (      ).

10.2 A major advantage of organoboron reagents is the exceptional configurational stability of their chiral carbon atoms, which enables metal-free stereospecific coupling reactions.
10.2.1 The reactivity of a boron reagent can be tuned by adding different nucleophiles. Among the ate complexes below, the bold C-B bond is most reactive in (      ) and least reactive in (      ).

(a) is 'CC1(C)O[B-](C)(OC)OC1(C)C'; (b) is 'CC1(C)O[B-](C)(N(C)C)OC1(C)C'; (c) is 'CC1(C)O[B-](C)(C)OC1(C)C'; and (d) is 'C[B-]1([C@@H]2CCC[C@H]1CCC2)C'. subquestions.text_open: 10.2.2 Write the SMILES representations of products A and B of the following reactions, including stereochemistry.

The reactant in the first is '[H][C@@](C1=CC=CC=C1)(C)B2OC(C)(C)C(C)(C)O2', and the conditions are MeONH_2, nBuLi, then Boc_2O; the unknown product is labeled A. The reactant in the second is 'CC(C(C)(C)O1)(C)OB1[C@](C2=CC=CC=C2)(C)CC', and the conditions are CH_2Cl_2, nBuLi, ZnCl_2, then NaOH/H_2O_2; the unknown product is labeled B.

subquestions.text_open: 10.2.3 An organoboron reagent treated with an aryllithium reagent can trap an electrophile. Experiments show, however, that different electrophiles give different stereochemical outcomes: the ate complex reacts with I_2 with good stereoselectivity, whereas reaction with DIAD results in extensive racemization. The researchers propose that the two reactions proceed by different mechanisms. Explain these observations mechanistically. Note: carbocations are planar, carbon-centered radicals undergo rapid configurational inversion, and carbanions have a high barrier to configurational inversion.

text_images.description: The image shows a multistep reaction in which the substrate is the same but the conditions differ. The substrate is 'C[C@H](B1OC(C)C(C)(C)O1)CCC2=CC=CC=C2'. The first-step conditions are 4-MeOC_6H_4Li, THF, -78°C, and the first-step product is 'C[C@H]([B-]1(C2=CC=C(OC)C=C2)OC(C)(C)C(C)(C)O1)CCC3=CC=CC=C3.[Li+]'. This product follows two pathways. The upper-right pathway uses I_2 and gives 'C[C@@H](I)CCC1=CC=CC=C1' with 97% enantioselectivity. The lower-right pathway uses DIAD, whose SMILES representation is 'O=C(/N=N/C(OC(C)C)=O)OC(C)C', and gives 'C[C@@H](N(NC(OC(C)C)=O)C(OC(C)C)=O)CCC1=CC=CC=C1' with 13% enantioselectivity.
